headline: Wisconsin Sen. LaTonya Johnson readies 2027 legalization bill
dek: Wisconsin Sen. LaTonya Johnson plans to refile adult-use legalization in 2027 with expungement, a medical programme and home grow, as Democrats take control.
key_points: State Sen. LaTonya Johnson (D-Milwaukee) is preparing to reintroduce comprehensive cannabis legalization in 2027, her office told The Marijuana Herald.
Her spokesman said the bill will include expungement of past convictions, a medical cannabis programme and protection for home cultivation.
Democrats take an 18-15 Senate and 53-46 Assembly majority in January, with Gov.-elect David Crowley backing legalization.
Wisconsin today allows only non-psychoactive CBD with a physician's certification, and a first possession offence remains a misdemeanour.
body: A Wisconsin legalization bill that stalled under Republican control is coming back, and this time its sponsor's party will be in the majority. State Sen. LaTonya Johnson, a Milwaukee Democrat, is preparing to reintroduce a comprehensive cannabis legalization bill in the 2027 session, her office told The Marijuana Herald in a report published on 24 November.

Jacob Taylor, Johnson's communications director, said the bill will carry expungement provisions, a medical cannabis programme and protections for home cultivation, and that her office is still working with partners on changes before the new year. No bill text or number has been released yet.
## What the bill is likely to contain

Johnson's last version, Senate Bill 1045, was introduced in February and would have legalized cannabis for adults 21 and over and created a regulated retail market, according to the Herald. It drew wide support from Democrats but did not advance in a Republican-controlled Legislature.

The 2027 version, as her office describes it, combines three things that are often split into separate bills elsewhere. Expungement would address past convictions. A medical programme would fill a gap that sets Wisconsin apart: it is one of the few states without a comprehensive medical cannabis law. Home cultivation would let adults grow their own, a provision that some recent legalization laws have left out or restricted.
> In Wisconsin the question for 2027 is no longer whether Democrats want legalization, but which bill becomes the vehicle and what Republicans demand for votes.

The November elections changed the arithmetic in Madison. Democrats will hold an 18-15 majority in the Senate and a 53-46 majority in the Assembly from January, according to the Herald, and Governor-elect David Crowley supports legalization. That gives Democrats control of both chambers and the governor's office for the first time since 2010.

Senior Democrats have already signalled intent. As the Herald reported on 12 November, incoming Assembly Speaker Greta Neubauer of Racine told reporters on 10 November that Democrats hope to pass legalization in the coming year. As we reported on 12 November, Crowley has pointed to cannabis tax revenue, which he has put at $80 million to $170 million a year, as one way to offset federal Medicaid cuts.

Republicans are not uniformly opposed. As we reported on 15 November, incoming Senate Republican Leader Julian Bradley has said he is open to discussing legalization. With an 18-15 Senate, Democrats can in principle pass a bill on their own votes, but a few defections would sink it, so Republican input could still shape the final text.

Neubauer, who has served in the Assembly since 2018 and currently leads the Democratic minority, was chosen unanimously by her caucus and is due to be formally elected on 4 January; she would be the first woman to serve as Wisconsin's Assembly speaker, the Herald reported. In February she told Spectrum News that Wisconsin residents had made clear they want access to both medical and adult-use cannabis. Together with Johnson's bill, that gives the incoming majority a sponsor, a speaker and a governor who all say they want the same outcome.

Wisconsin has no medical or adult-use cannabis law. Under a 2017 act, people with a physician's written certification may possess non-psychoactive CBD for any medical condition, but growing cannabis to make it is not allowed. A first possession offence is a misdemeanour carrying up to six months in jail and a $1,000 fine, and a repeat offence can be charged as a felony. Wisconsin has no citizen-initiative process, so any change must come through the Legislature.

Public support is broad. A Marquette Law School poll released in June 2025 found 67% of Wisconsin voters backed legalization, including 88% of Democrats and 79% of independents, the Herald reports. Three of Wisconsin's four neighbours, Illinois, Michigan and Minnesota, already allow adult-use sales, which means Wisconsin residents can drive across the border to buy legally and the tax revenue goes with them.

The new Legislature convenes in January, with the Assembly due to elect its speaker on 4 January. Watch for the release of Johnson's bill text and whether Democratic leaders adopt it as the caucus bill or start from a fresh draft; leaders have not yet decided whether legalization goes into the state budget or moves as a standalone bill. Also watch whether Republicans such as Bradley set conditions, for example a medical-first approach, that change what reaches the governor's desk.
